problem: Social navigation algorithms are each evaluated with ad-hoc scenarios, metrics and simulators, so methods cannot be compared consistently. Prior simulators usually drive pedestrians with synthetic models ('self-play' or 'against-all'), which treats a navigation model as ground-truth human behaviour. Prior dataset-replay evaluations give the robot no realistic sensor input and assume perfect perception.
motivation: Real-world user studies are expensive, hard to repeat, and limited in crowd size and context variety. Contrived real-world scenarios also make people behave unnaturally. The authors observe that replaying real pedestrian trajectories inside a photo-realistic simulator combines the realism of datasets with the repeatability and scale of simulation. A multi-axis metric suite then lets users weigh the efficiency-vs-pedestrian-disruption trade-off that fits their deployment context.
key_idea: SocNavBench is an algorithm-agnostic benchmark. It replays real ETH/UCY pedestrian trajectories (non-reactive) in rendered 3D environments across 33 curated episodes, and scores any navigation stack with a suite of path-quality, motion-quality, pedestrian-disruption and meta metrics.
insight:
The paper assumes that recorded pedestrian paths are the pedestrians' preferred paths, so collisions, low time-to-collision and small closest-pedestrian distance serve as proxies for socially disruptive behaviour. This assumption is argued to hold in dense, flow-dominated outdoor crowds (on average 44 pedestrians per episode), but not in narrow one-on-one negotiations such as a supermarket aisle. The case study shows that a single success number hides very different navigation styles:
- Social Forces is the most conservative: 32/33 successes and the fastest planning, but long, curved paths and the highest energy use (398.33 J).
- SA-CADRL is aggressive and goal-direct: the shortest paths and traversal times, but 40 pedestrian collisions and high jerk (31.68 m/s³). The authors attribute its collisions to crowd situations unseen in training, since the network only observes the 3 nearest pedestrians.
- ORCA sits in between: it reacts late, then backs away from approaching pedestrians, which gives it the longest traversal times.
- ORCA, CADRL and the baseline all have planning times close to each other, which shows that the shared meta-planner is the computational bottleneck.
method: Pedestrian replay: ETH and UCY trajectories are replayed 1:1 at the simulator tick rate (default 25 fps). Pedestrians do not react to the robot; collisions are registered but do not alter the replay.

Curated episodes: 33 hand-picked episodes of at most 60 s each, with 24–72 pedestrians (mean 44, SD 13) and semantically meaningful start/goal pairs in maps such as ETH, Univ, Zara and DoubleHotel. A random-episode sampler (goals reachable in 25 s at max velocity) supports learning.

Rendering: two modes. Schematic mode gives a top-down view with perfect perception of pedestrian positions. Full-render mode gives RGB-D from an arbitrary 6-DoF camera (default: on a Pioneer 3-DX), using the HumANav/Swiftshader renderer, SD3DIS building meshes modified to match the dataset sites, and 6000 SURREAL human meshes posed from recorded heading and speed.

Joystick API: a socket-based client/server interface runs a sense–plan–act cycle. It accepts velocity commands (3D unicycle kinematics) or position commands (velocity-limited holonomic mode). It runs synchronously (default, no penalty for thinking time) or asynchronously (real-time staleness).
Episode termination: an episode ends by Completion, Environment Collision or Timeout. Success means completion with no pedestrian collision.

Metrics suite: path quality (path length, path length ratio, path irregularity, goal traversal ratio, traversal time), motion quality (average speed, energy as ∫v² with unit mass, acceleration, jerk), pedestrian-related (closest-pedestrian distance saturated at 10 m; time-to-collision from linear extrapolation, saturated at 10 s), and meta statistics (success rate, T/PC/EC failure tuple, total pedestrian collisions, planning wait time).

Evaluated methods and baseline: the authors adapted Social Forces (PedSim), ORCA (pedestrian collaboration coefficient set to 0, robot to 1) and SA-CADRL (pre-trained 4-agent network fed the 3 nearest pedestrians). ORCA and CADRL are wrapped with a sampling meta-planner from HumANav/Tolani et al. that sets checkpoints on a 6 s horizon (4–7 m), reached within 1 m. The same meta-planner with unicycle kinematics serves as a pedestrian-unaware baseline.

setting.backbone: n/a (benchmark paper). Evaluated navigators: Social Forces (PedSim implementation), ORCA, SA-CADRL (authors' pre-trained 4-agent DRL network, frozen), and a pedestrian-unaware sampling meta-planner.
setting.training_data: none. The benchmark itself is not trained; SA-CADRL uses the original authors' pre-trained model. A random-episode sampler is provided for users who want to train.
setting.observation: Schematic mode (used in all experiments): ground-truth positions of all pedestrians plus the environment map. Full-render mode (available but not evaluated): RGB-D from a configurable 6-DoF camera.
setting.action_space: velocity commands under 3D unicycle kinematics, or velocity-limited holonomic position commands (max linear speed 1.2 m/s, Pioneer 3-DX specs). The social methods were run without kinematic constraints, only the max-speed limit.
setting.simulator: SocNavBench: a custom simulator built on the HumANav Swiftshader renderer, with SD3DIS meshes, SURREAL humans and ETH/UCY pedestrian replay.
setting.privileged: In the reported (Schematic) experiments, perfect perception: ground-truth positions of all pedestrians plus the environment map. ORCA and CADRL also rely on a meta-planner with map-based obstacle avoidance.

numbers_note:

They were run on the 33 curated SocNavBench episodes in Synchronous + Schematic mode, so they are excluded from 'numbers' per the no-baselines rule.

Metrics marked + (and Tables 3–4, unless noted) are computed on the 29/33 episodes completed by all four algorithms; the goal traversal ratio (−) uses only each algorithm's incomplete episodes. Pedestrian-disruption metrics (closest-pedestrian distance, TTC) are shown only as violin plots (Fig. 6), with no numbers.

Internal inconsistencies:
- Social Forces is listed with 1 total pedestrian collision in Table 2, but the text says it had 'no pedestrian collisions'.
- The baseline has 64 collisions in Table 2 but 'a total of 60 pedestrians across 23 episodes' in the text.
- Path length ratio is defined as straight-line / path length (higher = more direct), yet the printed values exceed 1, and the text treats higher values as more circuitous. It is effectively reported as path length / straight-line distance.
- The Table 2 header says planning wall time 'per episode', while Fig. 8 shows wait time per planning step.
results:
On 33 real-data episodes, Social Forces was the most successful (32/33 successes, no pedestrian-collision failures) and the fastest planner (18.23 s wall time per episode). It pays for this with long, curved paths and the highest energy use (398.33 J).
- ORCA: 24/33 successes, 15 pedestrian collisions.
- SA-CADRL: only 18/33, with 40 collisions across 14 episodes, despite being the most recent learned method; it had the shortest paths (15.70 m) and traversal times (15.14 s) but high jerk (31.68 m/s³).
- Pedestrian-unaware baseline: 9/33, 64 collisions, jerk 180.86 m/s³.
The authors conclude that SA-CADRL suits contexts where the robot has precedence (e.g. emergency deliveries) and Social Forces suits contexts where it must yield (e.g. a hospital laundry robot).
limitations: Pedestrians are non-reactive replays, so the benchmark cannot capture mutual negotiation of space; its metrics are poor proxies in sparse, narrow settings such as one pedestrian in an aisle or hallway.

All reported experiments use Schematic mode with perfect perception, and only 33 curated episodes from ETH/UCY (outdoor, fairly homogeneous) are evaluated. Only 3 classical or early-learning methods plus a baseline are tested, and SA-CADRL is restricted to the 3 nearest pedestrians and wrapped in an external meta-planner.

Metrics are automatic proxies with no human ratings of social acceptability. The reported tables contain internal inconsistencies: collision counts differ between table and text, and path length ratio values contradict its stated definition.
